definition: An architecture where clients send requests and a server processes them and returns responses; the server holds the shared state and logic.
The request-response application protocol of the web, built on methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), headers, status codes and an optional body.
HTTP carried over TLS, which encrypts the traffic and authenticates the server so that data cannot be read or tampered with in transit.
Transport Layer Security: the protocol that negotiates keys and encrypts a connection, using certificates to prove the server's identity.
Decrypting TLS at a proxy or load balancer so that backend servers receive plain traffic and do not each manage certificates.
A connection-oriented transport protocol that delivers bytes reliably and in order using handshakes, acknowledgements and retransmission.
A connectionless transport protocol that sends independent datagrams without ordering or delivery guarantees, trading reliability for low latency.
A transport protocol built on UDP that provides multiplexed streams, built-in encryption and faster connection setup; it is the basis of HTTP/3.
A binary version of HTTP that multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection and compresses headers, reducing connection overhead.
The version of HTTP that runs over QUIC instead of TCP, avoiding transport-level head-of-line blocking and speeding up connection setup.
A delay where one stalled item at the front of a queue or stream holds up everything behind it, such as a lost TCP packet stalling all multiplexed requests.
An API style that models data as resources addressed by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP methods, typically exchanging JSON.
A query language and API style in which clients specify exactly which fields they need from a typed schema, usually through a single endpoint.
A remote procedure call framework that uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for compact, strongly typed, streaming-capable service-to-service calls.
A protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent full-duplex channel so the server and client can push messages at any time.
A one-way streaming mechanism over HTTP in which the server pushes a continuous stream of text events to the browser, with automatic reconnection.
A client repeatedly asking the server whether anything new exists at a fixed interval; simple but wasteful and delayed by the interval.
A request that the server holds open until data is available or a timeout hits, after which the client immediately asks again.
The Domain Name System: a distributed, hierarchical database that resolves human-readable domain names to IP addresses, with heavy caching.
The duration for which a cached record or object may be reused before it must be refreshed, set for DNS records, cache entries and HTTP responses.
DNS that returns different answers depending on the requester's location so users are directed to the nearest data center or region.
Advertising the same IP address from many locations so network routing delivers each client to the topologically nearest one.
A content delivery network: geographically distributed edge servers that cache content close to users to cut latency and offload the origin.
A server placed near end users, typically in a CDN, that serves cached content and may run light logic before traffic reaches the origin.
The authoritative backend that holds the real content or computes the response; a CDN fetches from it on a cache miss.
An intermediary server that forwards requests between a client and a destination, adding functions such as caching, filtering or anonymity.
A proxy that sits in front of clients and makes outbound requests on their behalf, often for filtering, caching or hiding client identity.
A proxy that sits in front of servers and receives client requests on their behalf, handling TLS, caching, routing and load distribution.
A single entry point for clients that routes requests to backend services and centralizes concerns like authentication, rate limiting and request shaping.
A dedicated API layer tailored to one client type (web, mobile) that aggregates and shapes data from several backend services.
The time a single request takes from being sent to receiving its response, usually reported as percentiles such as p50 and p99.
The slowest fraction of requests (for example p99 or p99.9); it matters because a user request often fans out to many services and waits for the slowest.
The amount of work a system completes per unit of time, such as requests per second or megabytes per second.
The maximum rate at which data can be transferred over a link, measured in bits per second.
Queries (or requests) per second: the rate of incoming work, used to size servers, caches and databases; compare average QPS with peak QPS.
The time for a packet to travel to a destination and for the reply to return; connection setup and each chained request pay it again.
The fraction of network packets that never arrive; TCP retransmits them, which adds delay, while UDP simply drops them.
Variation in packet or response delay over time. In retries, the term also means random delay added to backoff to avoid synchronized clients.
A unique client-supplied token sent with a request so the server can recognize a retry and return the original result instead of repeating the action.
Splitting a large result set into pages returned one at a time, using offsets, page numbers or cursors.
Pagination that continues from an opaque marker pointing at the last item seen, which stays correct and fast when data changes between requests.
Evolving an API without breaking existing clients, commonly by putting a version in the URL, a header or the media type.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: a browser mechanism in which a server declares, via response headers, which other origins may read its responses.
Reusing one TCP (and TLS) connection for several requests, avoiding the cost of a new handshake for each.
Distributing traffic across regions or data centers, using DNS, anycast or a global proxy, based on proximity, health and capacity.
